source_text: Nec malum itaque naturale est, nec Deus creare reos potest, nec in regno diaboli collocare. Quibus collectis et tu Manichaeus, immo Manichaeo peior ostenderis; et sine peccato in hunc mundum humanitatis ingressus, et sub iure Dei, non diaboli, fructus fecunditatis, et naturalis innocentia claruerunt.
pass_a_gloss: Neither therefore is evil natural, nor can God create the guilty, nor collocate them in the kingdom of the devil. Which things having been gathered both you are shown a Manichaean, nay worse than a Manichaean; and without sin the entrance of humanity into this world, and under the right of God, not of the devil, the fruit of fecundity, and natural innocence have shone.

lemmas.lexica: LS naturalis; Blaise malum naturale=evil as a nature
LS/Blaise natura=created constitution, not 'original sin' itself
LS peccatum=fault, error; Blaise Christian sin
Blaise Manichaeus; Julian's polemic label vs natural evil
LS malum; Blaise malum naturale vs malum voluntatis

pass_b_english: Evil is therefore not inherent in nature, and God cannot create guilty people or place them in the devil's kingdom. These conclusions show you to be a Manichaean, indeed worse than a Manichaean. They also make clear that humanity enters this world without sin, that the fruit of human fertility is under God's authority rather than the devil's, and that nature is innocent.

choices.why: Julian's Manichaean charge: an evil that is a nature, not a will's act.
Julian's charge against Augustine: treating evil as a nature rather than as will.

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded.

speaker: Julian of Eclanum (words preserved in Augustine, Opus imperfectum contra Iulianum); Augustine's reply at this locus is excluded.
